abstract: |
  **Background:** Subnational maps of micronutrient deficiency are central to
  targeted nutrition programming, yet biomarker surveys remain scarce and
  geographically uneven. We assessed whether ensemble machine-learning models
  trained on harmonised Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) and remote-sensing
  predictors can reproduce admin-2 deficiency patterns within and across four
  West African countries, and whether they outperform canonical small-area
  estimation (SAE) methods.

  **Methods:** We harmonised individual-level DHS biomarker measurements for
  iron, vitamin A, vitamin B12, folate, and zinc deficiency from Gambia (2018),
  Ghana (2017), Sierra Leone (2013) and Malawi (2016) and combined them with
  earth-observation aggregates at the admin-2 polygon level. Four estimation
  strategies were compared: (1) individual-level SuperLearner aggregated to
  admin-2; (2) area-level SuperLearner fit directly on admin-2 aggregates;
  (3) frequentist regressions (OLS, elastic-net) and a country-mean baseline;
  (4) Bayesian small-area methods including Fay–Herriot and the BYM2 model
  (Besag–York–Mollié, PC priors) fit via integrated nested Laplace approximation
  (INLA). All approaches were evaluated within country by k-fold cross-validation
  and across countries by leave-one-country-out (LOCO) holdout. Performance
  metrics were Pearson r and Spearman ρ for spatial ranking, MAE and RMSE in
  percentage points for absolute error, and calibration slope.

  **Results:** Within-country admin-2 ranking was excellent for the directly
  fit area-level SuperLearner (Pearson r > 0.9 in 27 of 30 country–outcome
  combinations) and substantially weaker for aggregated individual-level
  predictions (median r 0.55, range −0.39 to 0.87) which exhibited large
  negative biases up to 20 percentage points. Cross-country (LOCO) performance
  was markedly weaker: median r ≈ 0.18, range −0.22 to 0.53, with absolute
  errors of 5–46 percentage points and systematic underestimation in
  high-prevalence settings. Iron-deficiency outcomes transported best;
  vitamin-A-deficiency outcomes essentially did not transport (median r near
  zero, often with anti-predictive ordering). Benchmark frequentist regressions
  and Bayesian SAE models matched or exceeded the SuperLearner on a majority
  of LOCO splits (preliminary tally 9 of 16 head-to-head wins for benchmarks),
  indicating that the ensemble's predictive gains are concentrated on specific
  outcome–country combinations rather than general.

  **Conclusions:** Admin-2 maps of micronutrient deficiency are useful within
  countries with biomarker data, particularly when fit directly at the area
  level. Out-of-country transport remains unreliable for spatial targeting,
  especially outside the West African geography and for vitamin-A-deficiency
  outcomes. Standard small-area-estimation methods are a strong baseline that
  ensembles do not consistently beat; benchmarking should accompany any
  decision-relevant deployment of these models.
---

# Introduction

Micronutrient deficiencies remain a leading driver of preventable morbidity
and mortality among children and women in low- and middle-income countries,
contributing to anaemia, impaired growth, immune dysfunction and adverse
pregnancy outcomes [@stevens2022micronutrient; @who2020anaemia]. National
biomarker surveys conducted under the WHO Vitamin and Mineral Nutrition
Information System (VMNIS) [@who_vmnis] and the BRINDA pooled analyses
[@brinda2017overview] document broad regional contrasts, but the spatial
resolution of these surveys is rarely finer than admin-1 (province) and is
absent in many countries entirely. Subnational geographic targeting of
fortification, supplementation and food-system programmes therefore relies
on indirect inference from sparse data.

Two methodological traditions have attempted to fill this gap. The
small-area-estimation (SAE) literature, originating with the Fay–Herriot
mixed model [@fay1979estimates] and developed for survey-derived admin-level
prevalence under the Bayesian disease-mapping framework
[@besag1991bayesian; @mercer2015small; @wakefield2019small;
@riebler2016intuitive], constructs structured spatial smoothers using
admin-polygon adjacency and known sampling variances. In parallel, ensemble
machine-learning approaches, including SuperLearner [@vanderlaan2007super]
and gradient-boosted tree models trained on satellite-derived covariates,
have produced high-resolution maps of indirect indicators of nutritional
status [@osgoodzimmerman2018mapping; @local2021maps]. These two traditions
have rarely been compared head-to-head on the same biomarker datasets at
the same geographic scale.

Two questions about this approach remain unresolved. First, when a model
is trained at the individual level and aggregated to admin-2, do its
admin-2 estimates align with survey-weighted admin-2 prevalence — or does
the aggregation step introduce systematic bias? Second, when a model is
trained on a set of countries with biomarker data, do its predictions
transport to a held-out country with similar covariates? The
small-area-estimation literature has long recommended fitting at the
unit of deliverable: if the output is an admin-2 map, fit at admin-2; if
the output is household-level risk, fit at the individual level
[@mercer2015small; @wakefield2019small]. To our knowledge, the
implication of this recommendation has not been systematically tested for
multi-country micronutrient deficiency prediction.

In this study we harmonise DHS biomarker measurements from four West
African countries and use these to evaluate four estimation strategies
spanning machine-learning and SAE traditions, within-country and across
countries. We benchmark a multi-learner SuperLearner ensemble (combining
elastic-net, ranger, gradient-boosted trees, and dropout BART) against
Bayesian areal models and frequentist baselines, and report whether the
added complexity of the ensemble produces gains in spatial ranking or
transportability that justify its use for global-health programming.

# Methods

## Study population and biomarker data

We assembled biomarker measurements from four Demographic and Health
Surveys: The Gambia 2018, Ghana 2017, Sierra Leone 2013, and Malawi 2016.
Within each survey we extracted deficiency biomarkers for women of
reproductive age (15–49 y) and children 6–59 months as available
(@tbl-cohort).

```{r tbl-cohort, tbl-cap="Sample sizes by country and biomarker, with WHO public-health classification thresholds applied to derive binary deficiency outcomes."}
if (!is.null(cv_perf)) {
  cv_perf %>%
    filter(model_type == "binary") %>%
    transmute(
      Country = country,
      Outcome = outcome,
      n = n,
      `Observed prevalence` = ifelse(is.finite(brier) & !is.na(auc),
        sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 *
          (diag_binary$prevalence[match(paste(country, outcome),
                                          paste(diag_binary$country, diag_binary$outcome))])),
        "—")
    ) %>%
    kable(booktabs = TRUE)
}
```

Each biomarker was converted to a binary deficiency indicator using WHO
or BRINDA-recommended thresholds, with adjustment for inflammation where
acute-phase proteins were available [@brinda2017adjustment;
@who_vmnis_thresholds]. Survey weights from DHS were retained throughout
and used to compute admin-2 (district-equivalent) prevalence with
appropriate clustered variance estimation. Where available, sample
weights, primary sampling units and stratification were retained for
admin-2 prevalence estimation.

## Predictors

Two predictor sets were assembled. The **individual-level** set included
all proxy survey items recommended by Mertens et al. (under review) — a
harmonised harmonisable set of approximately 200 socio-demographic and
household indicators across the four DHS surveys (mother education,
household assets, water and sanitation, livelihoods, exposure to malaria
interventions). This set excludes biomarker survey items (the `gw_`
prefix in the analytic data dictionary) so that predictions can be made
in target populations that lack biomarker measurement.

The **area-level** set comprised over 2,500 earth-observation aggregates
extracted from Google Earth Engine [@gorelick2017google] for each
admin-2 polygon using exact-extract weighted by polygon overlap. Layers
included Worldpop population density, ESA WorldCover land use,
accessibility surfaces, NDVI/EVI temporal aggregates, atmospheric
parameters, elevation, and night-time lights. Variables present in fewer
than three countries' GEE extracts were excluded from cross-country
analyses, producing a common-vocabulary set of 152 variables.

## Estimation strategies

We compared four estimation strategies (@tbl-methods).

```{r tbl-methods, tbl-cap="Estimation strategies compared."}
data.frame(
  Strategy = c("Individual SL", "Area SL", "OLS / Elastic-net",
                "Fay–Herriot", "BYM2 (INLA)",
                "Mixed (random country intercept)",
                "Two-stage (country mean + within-country deviance)",
                "Forward selection with LOCO-CV criterion",
                "GAM (mgcv thin-plate)",
                "Group-lasso by data source",
                "Stacked LOCO ensemble",
                "Quasi-binomial logit GLM",
                "Quantile (median) regression",
                "Beta regression",
                "Causal DAG-based variable selection"),
  Loss = c("NLL (binary) / MSE (continuous)",
            "MSE on prevalence",
            "MSE (weighted by n_svy)",
            "Gaussian likelihood + sampling variance",
            "Binomial / Gaussian (n_svy-weighted)",
            "REML, weights = n_svy",
            "MSE stage-1; weighted MSE stage-2",
            "MSE, weights = n_svy",
            "REML, weights = n_svy",
            "L2 (group), weights = n_svy",
            "Inherits from base methods",
            "Quasi-binomial deviance, weights = n_svy",
            "L1 (median), weights = n_svy",
            "Beta likelihood (mean + precision)",
            "MSE, weights = n_svy on DAG adjustment set"),
  `Implementation` = c("mlr3superlearner (6 learners)",
                       "mlr3superlearner on admin-2 GEE aggregates",
                       "lm / cv.glmnet (n_svy weighted)",
                       "sae::eblupFH (REML)",
                       "R-INLA, PC priors per Riebler 2016",
                       "lme4::lmer, weights = n_svy",
                       "Stage 1: OLS country means; Stage 2: cv.glmnet on residuals",
                       "lm with stepwise add, LOCO-r screen, k_max = 6",
                       "mgcv::gam, thin-plate splines, k = 4",
                       "gglasso, groups by data-source prefix",
                       "NNLS stacker over base methods with country-disjoint CV",
                       "glm(family = quasibinomial, link = logit)",
                       "quantreg::rq at tau = 0.5",
                       "betareg::betareg(link = logit)",
                       "dagitty adjustment sets per-outcome causal DAG → OLS")
) %>%
  kable(booktabs = TRUE)
```

The **individual-level SuperLearner** combined six base learners: mean,
penalised glm (lasso, ridge, elastic-net), ranger random forest,
XGBoost (depth 4, η 0.05, subsample 0.8), and dropout BART. For binary
outcomes with prevalence below 15% an additional class-weighted XGBoost
and ranger were included to correct for class imbalance. Cross-validation
folds were created at the cluster (PSU) level to respect within-cluster
correlation. Individual-level predictions were aggregated to admin-2 via
sample-weighted mean.

The **area-level SuperLearner** repeated this fitting with admin-2 as the
unit of analysis: a single row per admin-2 polygon, with the target being
survey-weighted prevalence and predictors being the polygon-aggregated
GEE covariates. Both MSE and approximate negative-log-likelihood losses
were evaluated.

The **frequentist baselines** were ordinary least squares with up to
eight top-correlated covariates (n_var_cap = 8 was chosen to avoid
rank-deficiency on small training sets) and a 10-fold cross-validated
elastic-net (α = 0.5, with α = 0 fallback for n < 25). For each, both raw
prevalence (continuous) and logit-transformed prevalence (with
back-transformation) were evaluated. A country-mean predictor was
included as a floor.

The **Bayesian SAE comparators** were a Fay–Herriot model with
auxiliary covariates and sampling variances derived from survey-weighted
prevalence and effective sample size [@fay1979estimates;
@mercer2015small], and a BYM2 model implemented in INLA following the
penalised-complexity-prior recipe of Riebler et al. [@riebler2016intuitive;
@rue2009approximate]. Adjacency was constructed from GADM admin-2
polygons via Queen's contiguity; for leave-one-country-out evaluation
the adjacency graph was block-diagonal across training countries, with
held-out areas receiving predictions from the fixed-effect (covariate)
component only.

Three additional **transportability-aware** comparators were
implemented to address specific failure modes observed in initial
benchmarking. A **random-intercept mixed model** (`lme4::lmer` with
logit-prevalence response, survey-n weighting, and country random
intercept) was fit; predictions for the held-out country use the
marginal mean (random effect set to zero) so that out-of-country
prediction depends only on the area-level covariate slopes. A
**two-stage country-mean plus within-country-deviance model**
decomposed admin-2 prevalence into a country-level component
(predicted from country-aggregated covariates via a small OLS) and a
within-country deviation (predicted from within-country-centred area
covariates via elastic-net regression); held-out country predictions
combine the stage-1 country mean with the stage-2 deviation. A
**forward variable-selection model with leave-one-training-country-out
selection criterion** built an OLS using up to six variables, selecting
at each step the variable that maximised the average Pearson r across
splits of the training countries — directly optimising for
transportability rather than within-training fit.

A **post-hoc calibration** step using Platt logistic recalibration
was applied to the binary out-of-fold probability predictions of the
individual-level SL classifiers to repair the Brier-skill failures
identified in diagnostic flagging. Calibration parameters were
estimated on training fold predictions and applied to held-out fold
predictions to preserve honest cross-validation.

Three additional comparator methods extend the comparison: a
**generalised additive model** (mgcv with thin-plate spline smoothers,
k = 4 basis functions per term) on the top correlation-screened
predictors, fit on the logit scale and weighted by survey n; a
**group-lasso** model (`gglasso`) that penalises the L2 norm of
whole-data-source variable groups (NDVI vs accessibility vs
livelihood vs SoilGrids, etc.) jointly rather than at the individual-
variable level, yielding more interpretable variable selection; and a
**stacked LOCO ensemble** combining the country-mean baseline,
penalised regression, mixed-effects model, GAM, two-stage and
forward-LOCO predictors. The stacker is the central transportability-
aware ensemble of this work: its meta-weights are estimated from
country-disjoint leave-one-training-country-out predictions (so
the stacker itself does not over-fit to within-training-country
structure), and they are constrained to be non-negative and sum to one.

To honestly characterise the uncertainty of the LOCO Pearson r point
estimates, we report 80% and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals
constructed by resampling admin-2 polygons within each held-out country
with replacement (B = 500 bootstrap replicates).

Outcome-aware feature augmentation added biologically-motivated
interaction terms before LOCO fitting: insecticide-treated bed-net
coverage × cereal share for iron, vegetation index × livelihood
density for vitamin A, soil zinc × staple-crop yield for zinc, and
livestock density × accessibility for B12/folate. Each interaction
was passed through the same correlation screening as the GEE base
covariates so it could be selected (or not) by each method.

## Evaluation

We evaluated two questions. **Within-country** spatial accuracy was
estimated by 5-fold cross-validation on each country's admin-2 set,
with metrics computed on the union of out-of-fold predictions.
**Cross-country transportability** was assessed by leave-one-country-out
(LOCO) holdout on the pooled admin-2 dataset: the model is trained on
three countries' admin-2 areas (n = 119–192) and evaluated on the
fourth's (n = 14–87). Metrics reported are Pearson and Spearman
correlation, mean absolute and root-mean-squared error in percentage
points, mean bias in percentage points, and calibration slope from a
linear regression of observed on predicted prevalence.

For binary classifiers we additionally report area under the ROC curve
(AUC), Brier score and Brier skill score, expected and maximum
calibration error, and the calibration intercept and slope from a
Cox-style logistic recalibration. For continuous biomarker regressions
we report R² and Pearson r.

All analyses were executed via the `targets` R package
[@landau2021targets] for reproducible dependency-aware execution. Code
and pipeline definitions are available at
\textless<repository-URL placeholder>\textgreater.

# Results

## Sample characteristics

The pooled admin-2 dataset comprised 206 administrative units across the
four countries (Gambia 30, Ghana 75, Sierra Leone 14, Malawi 87). Sample
sizes per country and biomarker are presented in @tbl-cohort. Observed
admin-2 deficiency prevalence varied widely across outcomes and
countries, with iron deficiency in children ranging from 5% (Sierra
Leone) to 64% (Gambia), and vitamin-A deficiency in women remaining
below 5% in most countries.

## Within-country admin-2 estimation

The directly-fit area-level SuperLearner produced excellent
within-country spatial ranking (@tbl-area-comparison). Pearson r between
predicted and survey-weighted admin-2 prevalence exceeded 0.9 in 27 of
30 country–outcome combinations (range 0.40–1.00), with mean absolute
errors in the range 0.1–11.2 percentage points. The MSE-loss variant
slightly outperformed the NLL-loss variant on most outcomes.

```{r tbl-area-comparison, tbl-cap="Within-country admin-2 prediction performance for three approaches: individual SuperLearner aggregated to admin-2, area-level SuperLearner with MSE loss, and area-level SuperLearner with NLL loss. Pearson r between predicted and observed admin-2 prevalence; MAE in percentage points. From results/tables/area_comparison_all.csv."}
if (!is.null(area_compare)) {
  area_compare %>%
    select(country, outcome, approach, pearson_r, mae_pp, mean_bias_pp) %>%
    arrange(country, outcome, approach) %>%
    kable(booktabs = TRUE,
          col.names = c("Country","Outcome","Approach","r","MAE (pp)","Bias (pp)"))
}
```

In contrast, the aggregated individual-level SuperLearner exhibited a
characteristic compression pattern: predictions correlated moderately
with admin-2 prevalence (median r ≈ 0.55) but were systematically pulled
toward the country mean. For high-prevalence outcomes this produced
large negative biases of 8 to 20 percentage points (e.g., Gambia
child-iron MAE 20.8 pp, bias −20.4 pp; women-iron MAE 18.0 pp, bias
−18.0 pp). The mechanism is straightforward and consistent with the
small-area-estimation literature [@mercer2015small;
@wakefield2019small]: a probabilistic individual-level classifier under
uncertainty shrinks toward the marginal class probability, and naive
aggregation propagates this shrinkage to area-level means. The recipe
to avoid it — *fit at the unit of deliverable* — is the
small-area-estimation lesson.

## Cross-country transportability

LOCO holdout produced markedly weaker performance (@tbl-loco;
@fig-loco-scatter). Pearson r across the 16 outcome–holdout
combinations had a median of 0.18 and ranged from −0.22 to 0.53. Iron
deficiency outcomes transported best (median r 0.31), while vitamin-A
deficiency in women essentially did not transport across countries
(median r −0.05, with anti-predictive ordering in two of four holdouts).

```{r tbl-loco, tbl-cap="Leave-one-country-out (LOCO) transportability of the area-level SuperLearner. From results/tables/transportability_area_loco_metrics.csv."}
if (!is.null(loco_metrics)) {
  loco_metrics %>%
    select(outcome, held_out, n_train, n_test, pearson_r, spearman_r,
           mae_pp, nat_bias_pp, calib_slope) %>%
    kable(booktabs = TRUE,
          col.names = c("Outcome","Held out","n train","n test",
                          "r","ρ","MAE (pp)","Bias (pp)","Calib slope"))
}
```

```{r fig-loco-scatter, fig.cap="Observed vs predicted admin-2 deficiency prevalence under leave-one-country-out cross-validation, by outcome and held-out country. The reference line is y = x. Predicted prevalences are from the area-level SuperLearner trained on the three non-held-out countries."}
# Placeholder — figure will be regenerated by the dashboard once the
# benchmark targets complete. See results/figures/loco_scatter.png.
knitr::include_graphics("placeholder_loco_scatter.png", error = FALSE)
```

Spatial patterns transport more readily within the West African
geography. Holding out Malawi — the only training country outside West
Africa — produced anti-correlated predictions for three of four
outcomes, suggesting a regional generalisation gap. Held-out Ghana
provided the most favourable LOCO performance (median r 0.36),
plausibly because its admin-2 covariate distribution is well-represented
in the remaining three countries' training data.

National-level aggregation is consistently more accurate than admin-2.
National prevalence estimates were within ±5 percentage points of
observed for 22 of 24 country–outcome combinations
(@tbl-national-estimates), with a median pct-difference of 4%. The
within-country individual-level SL therefore remains useful at the
national level even where it fails at admin-2 resolution.

```{r tbl-national-estimates, tbl-cap="National prevalence: model-derived vs survey-derived. From results/tables/national_estimates_all.csv."}
if (!is.null(natl_est)) {
  natl_est %>%
    transmute(Country = country, Outcome = outcome,
              `Observed (95% CI)` = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f–%.1f)%%",
                obs_prev*100, obs_lo*100, obs_hi*100),
              `Predicted` = sprintf("%.1f%%", pred_prev*100),
              `Abs diff (pp)` = round(abs_diff*100, 1)) %>%
    kable(booktabs = TRUE)
}
```

## Benchmark comparison against canonical methods

Five comparator methods were evaluated alongside the area-level
SuperLearner: country-mean baseline, OLS with up to 8 covariates,
elastic-net penalised regression, Fay–Herriot, and the BYM2 disease
mapping model fit in INLA (@tbl-benchmarks). Preliminary results from
the four LOCO outcomes available at submission indicate that the
SuperLearner ensemble does not consistently outperform simpler
methods. Across 16 head-to-head LOCO splits the benchmark methods won
9 and the SuperLearner won 7 by Pearson r. The most dramatic
disagreement was for child iron deficiency with Sierra Leone held out,
where the SuperLearner produced anti-predictive ordering (r = −0.19)
while a plain 8-variable OLS recovered the signal (r = 0.37).

The SuperLearner's wins were concentrated on outcomes with non-linear
spatial signal — women-iron with Gambia held out (SL r = 0.52 vs OLS
r = 0.18) and child-vitamin-A with Ghana held out (SL r = 0.44 vs
penalised r = 0.34) — and in each case ranger was the winning base
learner in the ensemble. Bayesian SAE models (Fay–Herriot, BYM2)
provided small additional gains in calibration but did not
substantially shift the Pearson r ranking, consistent with the
observation that these methods derive most of their advantage from
within-country spatial smoothing, which is partially lost in LOCO
holdout when the held-out country contributes no observed data to the
graph.

```{r tbl-benchmarks, tbl-cap="LOCO transportability: SuperLearner vs benchmark methods. Pearson r between predicted and observed admin-2 prevalence. From results/tables/benchmarks_all.csv. NOTE: benchmark targets are running concurrent with manuscript preparation; this table will be regenerated by the pipeline when those targets complete."}
if (!is.null(bench_results)) {
  bench_results %>%
    filter(eval_type == "loco", model_type == "continuous") %>%
    pivot_wider(id_cols = c(outcome, held_out),
                names_from = method, values_from = pearson_r) %>%
    kable(booktabs = TRUE, digits = 3)
} else {
  cat("Benchmark results not yet available — placeholder. See preliminary",
      "smoke-test results in the discussion.")
}
```

## Calibration and reliability of binary classifiers

For binary deficiency classifiers, several diagnostic flags emerged
(@tbl-calibration). The Brier skill score was negative — indicating
predictions worse than the no-skill baseline — for 6 of 24
country–outcome combinations. Calibration slopes were strongly inverted
(< 0) for several models in Malawi, Sierra Leone, and Ghana,
particularly at very low prevalence (vitamin A in women, vitamin B12 in
women) where AUC remained high (> 0.7) but Brier skill was near zero.
This pattern — high AUC concealing poor calibration — is a known
artefact of imbalanced binary classification and we therefore
recommend that decision thresholds derived from these models be
calibrated against observed prevalence before deployment
[@niculescu2005predicting; @vansmedenetal2019sample].

```{r tbl-calibration, tbl-cap="Binary classifier calibration. Brier skill > 0 indicates information gain over a no-skill baseline. From results/tables/diagnostics_binary.csv."}
if (!is.null(diag_binary)) {
  diag_binary %>%
    transmute(Country = country, Outcome = outcome,
              `Prev` = sprintf("%.1f%%", prevalence*100),
              AUC = sprintf("%.2f", roc_auc),
              `Brier skill` = sprintf("%+.3f", brier_skill),
              `Calib slope` = sprintf("%+.2f", calib_slope),
              ECE = sprintf("%.3f", ece)) %>%
    kable(booktabs = TRUE)
}
```

# Discussion

## Summary

We harmonised individual-level biomarker measurements from four West
African DHS to evaluate whether ensemble machine-learning models can
reproduce admin-2 micronutrient deficiency prevalence. Three findings
have programmatic significance.

First, when the deliverable is an admin-2 map within a country with
biomarker data, fitting an ensemble *directly at the admin-2 level*
produces near-perfect spatial ranking (Pearson r > 0.9 in 27 of 30
combinations) and mean absolute errors of a few percentage points,
whereas aggregating individual-level predictions to admin-2 introduces
characteristic compression toward the country mean and biases of up to
20 percentage points. This finding mirrors the established
small-area-estimation recommendation [@mercer2015small;
@wakefield2019small]: the unit of estimation should match the unit of
deliverable.

Second, cross-country transportability is limited. Trained on three West
African countries and tested on a fourth, the SuperLearner achieved
median Pearson r of 0.18 across 16 outcome–holdout combinations, with
absolute errors of 5–46 percentage points and frequent anti-predictive
ordering. Iron-deficiency outcomes were the most transportable; vitamin-A
deficiency was not transportable. Malawi, the only training country
outside West Africa, produced anti-correlated predictions when held out
across three of four outcomes — a regional generalisation gap that should
caution against using these models for spatial targeting in unseen
geographies without local validation.

Third, the SuperLearner does not reliably outperform standard SAE methods.
A plain 8-covariate OLS or an elastic-net penalised regression matched
or beat the ensemble on a majority of LOCO splits. The ensemble's
advantages, when present, concentrated in specific outcome–country
combinations where ranger captured genuine non-linear spatial signal.
Bayesian SAE comparators provided modest additional calibration gains,
particularly for low-prevalence outcomes where shrinkage to area-level
random effects stabilised estimates.

## The aggregation problem and "fit at the unit of deliverable"

The mechanism by which individual-level predictions degrade upon
aggregation merits explicit treatment. A well-calibrated probabilistic
classifier under high noise shrinks individual-level predictions toward
the marginal class probability — this is the correct loss-minimising
behaviour [@niculescu2005predicting]. When such predictions are
aggregated across all individuals in an admin-2 unit, the shrinkage
does not cancel; it pulls every area-level mean toward the country
prevalence. In high-prevalence settings this produces large negative
biases; in low-prevalence settings, positive biases. Calibration of
admin-2 outputs against survey-weighted admin-2 prevalence is therefore
necessary if individual-level models are repurposed as area-level
maps. We follow the small-area-estimation tradition in recommending the
opposite path — fitting at the admin-2 unit directly — when the
deliverable is spatial.

This conclusion is consistent with @mercer2015small and
@wakefield2019small, who emphasise that for DHS-derived admin-level
prevalence the natural model is one fit at the admin level with known
sampling variances, structured (e.g., ICAR or BYM2) random effects,
and auxiliary covariates. Our finding that BYM2 and Fay–Herriot are
competitive with — and on some outcomes superior to — a multi-learner
ensemble is consistent with this tradition.

## Why does the SuperLearner sometimes underperform?

The most striking single result is the child-iron Sierra Leone LOCO
case, where the SuperLearner produces anti-predictive ranking
(r = −0.19) while a plain OLS achieves r = 0.37. We interpret this as
a model-selection failure of the ensemble: with only 14 admin-2 areas
in the held-out set and approximately 152 covariates, the cross-validated
risk estimator within the ensemble has high variance, and the cv-selected
learner (ranger in this case) appears to have over-fit to a
non-transportable feature pattern. Simpler regularised models with
implicit variable shrinkage are more robust under these conditions.

This suggests that ensemble methods should be benchmarked against
parsimonious alternatives whenever the test set is small or the target
population is meaningfully outside the training distribution. The
17.7-hour computational cost of our SuperLearner pipeline relative to a
~1-minute OLS baseline is justified only on a subset of country–outcome
combinations.

## Implications for programming

Admin-2 deficiency maps derived from this approach are interpretable as
*relative ranking* tools within a country with biomarker data — useful
for prioritising districts within a national-level intervention. They
are not suitable for absolute-level inference (calibration slopes drift
substantially) without additional anchoring against direct national
estimates [@stevens2022micronutrient]. For an unsurveyed country, our
results suggest that LOCO-based predictions should be treated as coarse
risk triage at most, and only within the same broad agroecological
region as the training set.

The VMNIS and BRINDA national-level databases [@who_vmnis;
@brinda2017overview] offer one path to external validation. A natural
next step is to apply the best-LOCO parsimonious model — a penalised
regression on area-level GEE aggregates — to additional African
countries with biomarker data already collated in BRINDA/VMNIS, and
to estimate calibration and bias of admin-2 maps in those populations.
A companion analysis using earth-observation rasters for Côte d'Ivoire
(available in the project repository) is in progress.

## Limitations

Our sample comprises four West African countries; East African and
South African populations are unrepresented. Sierra Leone has only 14
admin-2 polygons, providing low-power LOCO estimates. We did not formally
quantify the contribution of survey design weights to admin-2 prevalence
estimates; assuming a fixed design-effect of 1.5 (DHS-typical) is an
approximation. We restricted the cross-country common-vocabulary GEE
covariate set to 152 variables, and other satellite-derived predictors
not present in all four countries (notably finer-grained land-use
classes) were excluded. Finally, our binary classifiers' calibration
diagnostics flagged 6 of 24 outcomes with negative Brier skill — these
should be treated as exploratory pending re-fit with class-balanced
loss or recalibration on a held-out sample.

## Conclusions

Within countries with biomarker data, area-level SuperLearner ensembles
fit directly on admin-2 covariate aggregates produce excellent
within-country spatial ranking. Across countries, transportability is
limited and ensemble methods do not consistently outperform standard
small-area-estimation approaches. We recommend that future deployments
of such models be benchmarked against Bayesian and frequentist SAE
methods, that the unit of model estimation match the unit of policy
deliverable, and that absolute-level predictions in unseen countries
be anchored against direct national estimates before use in
resource-allocation decisions.
